title: Statistical Methods and Results for grasshopper Range Analysis
text:
All statistics were conducted in R version 4.5.2 (2025-10-31) (R Core Team, 2024) using generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) and generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) implemented with mgcv (Wood 2017, 2011, 2004) and glmmTMB (Brooks et al. 2017; McGillycuddy et al. 2025) packages, respectively. Models were appriased/validated using DHARMa (Hartig 2024) and gratia (Simpson 2024). Model selection when needed was done using AIC. Estimated marginal means and pairwise comparisons were calculated using the emmeans package (Lenth and Piaskowski 2025). Data visualization was performed using the ggplot2 package (Wickham 2016) along with extensions from the tidyverse suite of packages (Wickham et al. 2019). All code and data are versioned on github at: github.com/ddlawton/OSE-Range-Analysis. Upon publication a github archive snapshot will be created and stored in Zenodo for reproducibility with a DOI and citation.
Throughout this manuscript, significance is denoted using asterisks: *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, * p < 0.05.



Maps of mean annual precipitation (MAP) and monthly rainfall patterns were generated using Climate Hazards Center Infrared Precipitation with Stations (CHIRPS) data (Funk et al. 2015) processed in Google Earth Engine (Gorelick et al. 2017) and imported into R for visualization with the terra (Hijmans 2025) and tidyterra (Hernangómez 2023) packages. Senegal administrative boundaries were obtained from the Natural Earth public domain map dataset using the rnaturalearth package (Massicotte and South 2025).



For both density and damage, separate models were created for each of the three survey missions to assess how effects changed over time relative to the timing of fertilizer application. We specified the models as generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) with a Poisson family for density and a tweedie family for damage percent. In both cases, we included fertilizer treatment, region, and their interaction as fixed effects, and farmer as a random effect to account for repeated measures since each farmer has a control and fertilized field.
Data adjustments: The OSE density data (ose_count) received from collaborators had already been adjusted for the proportion of OSE in the total grasshopper population, which is appropriate for density analysis. For damage analysis, we reversed this adjustment to represent total grasshopper damage rather than OSE-specific damage, maintaining consistency with our previous publications. The adjustment used region-specific OSE proportions averaged across missions: Kaffrine = 0.93, Fatick = 0.91, Thies = 0.79, Saint Louis = 0.65.



For millet yield, we specified a GLMM with a tweedie family to account for the continuous, positive, and right-skewed nature of yield data. Like the locust density and damage models, we included fertilizer treatment, region, and their interaction as fixed effects, and farmer as a random effect to account for repeated measures.



To test whether the effect of fertilizer on grasshopper density is mediated by ground cover, we fit a unified generalized additive model (GAM) with a Tweedie family to account for overdispersed count data. The model included fertilizer treatment, mission number, their interaction, and region as fixed effects, a random effect for farmer, and, critically, a by-variable smooth term allowing the relationship between ground cover and grasshopper density to vary by fertilizer treatment. Constructing a unified model allowed as to look directly at the mediation effect of ground cover on the fertilizer treatment effect on grasshopper density while accounting for the main effects of fertilizer treamtment and mission.

section: 2.2 Locust developmental stages and generations through space and time
text:
2.2 Locust developmental stages and generations through space and time
The locust surveys enabled us to identify the developmental stages and likely generations of Oedaleus senegalensis present during each mission (?@tbl-dev-stages). We identified three generations (G1, originating from the eggs of the previous season’s last generation, and G2 and G3) in the Thies, Fatick, and Kaffrine regions. In Saint Louis, only the G1 and G2 generations were observed. All developmental stages were identified, from eggs, through nymphal instars (1-5), to adults.

title: Statistical Methods and Results for grasshopper Range Analysis
text:
2.3 Crop impact

2.3.1 Senegalese grasshopper density
Fertilizer treatment progressively suppressed grasshopper density over the growing season, with effects intensifying from non-significant early in the season (Mission 1: p = 0.093) to highly significant by late season (Mission 3: estimate = -1.374, p < 0.001; Table 2). This temporal pattern reflected both fertilizer application and cumulative grasshopper population suppression. Regional responses varied significantly, with Kaffrine showing consistently elevated densities across all treatments and missions. By mission 3, grasshopper densities in control fields were 3.4-times higher than in fertilized fields in Kaffrine and -times higher in Thiès. Across all missions, the suppressive effect of fertilization in Kaffrine ranged from 1.1–3.4-fold (Table 3).


2.3.2 Grasshopper damage to millet
Crop damage mirrored grasshopper density patterns, intensifying throughout the missions and showing strongest fertilizer suppression by mission 3 (estimate = -2.384, p < 0.001; Table 4). Control fields had 3–11 times higher damage than fertilized fields by the last mission, with effects particularly pronounced in Fatick and Kaffrine (Table 5).


2.3.3 Millet yield
Fertilizer treatment significantly increased millet yield across all harvested regions (estimate = 0.603, p < 0.001), with the strongest effect in Thiès (p not available; Table 6, Table 7). Control fields had 55% lower yield than fertilized fields in Fatick and Kaffrine, representing an approximately 1.8-fold increase from fertilization. Saint Louis was excluded from yield analysis due to insufficient rainfall for crop maturation.

title: Statistical Methods and Results for grasshopper Range Analysis
section: 2.8 Ground Cover Mediation of Fertilizer Effects on grasshopper Density
text:
2.8 Ground Cover Mediation of Fertilizer Effects on grasshopper Density
Ground cover mediated fertilizer effects on grasshopper density differently between treatments (deviance explained: 64%; Table 8). In fertilized fields, density peaked at ~40% ground cover and declined at higher and lower values, whereas control fields showed low densities until 60–70% cover, after which densities increased substantially.








Figure 7: Senegalese grasshopper density peaked at around 40% ground cover in fertilized fields and around 60-70% in control fields. However, ground cover did not differ significantly between fertilizer treatments. See Supp. Tables SX and SX for full statistical analysis and Supp. Fig. SX for raw data points.

text:
3.2 Ground Cover by Fertilizer Treatment








Figure 9: Ground cover by fertilizer treatment and mission across regions. Ground cover increased throughout the growing season across all regions, with minimal differences between control and fertilized treatments. Statistical analysis (Table 1) confirmed no significant main effect of fertilizer or fertilizer × mission interaction.

title: Statistical Methods and Results for grasshopper Range Analysis
section: 3.3 Temperature Variation Across Missions and Regions
text:
3.3 Temperature Variation Across Missions and Regions








Figure 10: Temperature variation across missions and regions. Fatick showed increasing temperature through the sampling period, while Kaffrine, Thiès, and Saint-Louis remained more stable. Saint-Louis was generally cooler than the other regions. These patterns suggest that temperature at the time of survey is not a primary driver of grasshopper counts once region and mission timing are accounted for.

title: Managing the Senegalese Grasshopper Through Soil Fertility Enhancement
text:
Study Design
During the 2021 growing season (July–October), 250 farmers participated in a paired-field experiment where each managed:

One fertilized field receiving 150 kg each of NPK and urea
One non-fertilized control field

Each field was surveyed three times to record:

Grasshopper density and developmental stage
Vegetation cover and temperature
Millet yield at harvest
OSE damage to millet leaves (percent leaf damage)

Total Coverage: 500 ha across 1,500 sampling points in four regions (Fatick, Kaffrine, Thiès, and Saint-Louis)

title: Managing the Senegalese Grasshopper Through Soil Fertility Enhancement
text:
Computational Architecture
This project uses a targets pipeline for reproducible computation with clean separation of concerns:

Key Principles

Separation of Computation and Presentation

_targets.R: ALL data processing, modeling, and post-processing
Quarto documents: ONLY import artifacts and create visualizations

Reproducibility Through Targets

Incremental builds track dependencies automatically
Models cached intelligently based on code/data changes
Run targets::tar_make() to execute the entire pipeline




Statistical Framework
All analyses were conducted in R using:

Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) via glmmTMB for locust density, damage, and yield outcomes
Generalized Additive Mixed Models (GAMMs) via mgcv for non-linear relationships with environmental covariates
Model validation using DHARMa and gratia
Estimated marginal means and pairwise comparisons via emmeans



Code Organization
The analysis follows a targets-based modular architecture:
Pipeline Layer (_targets.R):

Orchestrates all computational work
Defines dependencies between targets
Manages incremental builds and caching

Function Layer (R/functions/):

data_preprocessing.R: Data loading, cleaning, validation
statistical_models.R: Model fitting functions for GLMMs and GAMs
plotting_functions.R: Publication-ready visualizations
figure_export.R: File I/O utilities for saving outputs
senegal_map.R: Geographic mapping functions
table_variable_summary.R: Summary table generation

Presentation Layer (R/analysis/*.qmd):

Quarto documents that import pre-computed artifacts
Load models from data/model_objects/*.rds
Import tables from outputs/tables/*.csv
Create inline statistics and format results for publication
Generate final figure compositions



Targets Pipeline Workflow
The _targets.R pipeline orchestrates all computation in three stages:
Stage 1: Data Preparation

Load raw Excel data
Clean and validate fields
Create analysis-ready datasets

Stage 2: Statistical Modeling

Fit GLMMs for locust density (3 missions) and damage (3 missions)
Fit GLMMs for yield outcomes
Fit GAMs for ground cover mediation and temperature effects
Save all models to data/model_objects/*.rds

Stage 3: Post-Processing

Generate emmeans and pairwise comparisons
Create model diagnostic plots
Export summary tables as CSV
Save high-resolution figures



Manuscript Methods and Results
The Methods and Results page contains the final statistical models, results, and figures used in the manuscript submission.


Exploratory Work
The Exploratory Work section provides detailed analyses that informed the manuscript, including:

Data summaries and regional maps
Individual analyses for locust density, damage, and yield
Environmental covariate relationships
Gender dynamics in farmer participation

These exploratory pages document the full analytical process and provide transparency into our statistical decision-making. Not all exploratory analyses appear in the final manuscript.

title: Basic Statistics and Maps
text:
Mean Annual Precipitation (MAP)
Mean annual precipitation (MAP) for Senegal was calculated using the CHIRPS dataset, which provides high-resolution (approximately 5 km) gridded precipitation estimates. We extracted CHIRPS daily precipitation data for Senegal for the most recent 10-year period (2015–2024). The data were spatially clipped to the national boundary, summed annually, and then averaged across years to produce a single raster layer representing mean annual precipitation.

title: 2021 Locust × Ground Cover
text:
Overview
This analysis explores how locust (OSE) density is influenced by ground cover across different regions and fertilizer treatments. We use generalized additive models (GAMs) with a Tweedie family distribution to handle the overdispersed count data.

title: 2021 Locust × Ground Cover
text:
Model Specification
\[
\begin{align*}
\text{ose\_count}_i &= \alpha + f(\text{percent\_ground\_cover}_i, \text{region\_treat}_i) + b_{\text{farmer}_i} + \varepsilon_i
\end{align*}
\]
where:

\(\alpha\) is the intercept,
\(f(\text{percent\_ground\_cover},\, \text{region\_treat})\) is a smooth function (tensor product, using factor-smooth interaction) over percent ground cover and region treatment,
\(b_{\text{farmer}_i}\) is a random effect for each farmer,
\(\varepsilon_i\) is the residual error.

title: 2021 Locust × Ground Cover
text:
Model Fitting
The unified ground cover mediation model is a GAM with by-variable smooths that allows the relationship between ground cover and OSE density to vary by fertilizer treatment. Diagnostics look good:

title: 2021 Locust × Ground Cover
text:
Model Results
The unified model shows how ground cover mediates fertilizer effects on OSE density. The smoothed relationships show different patterns between control and fertilized treatments.
Note: These results may differ from earlier manuscript versions due to data processing differences.

Peak Densities:

Fertilized plots: OSE counts peak at approximately 40% ground cover
Control plots: OSE counts peak at approximately 60–70% ground cover

Mechanism: Fertilizer treatment likely modifies OSE responses through:

Changes in crop vigor and nutritional quality
Altered plant species composition
Modified microclimate conditions




Implications
The interaction between fertilizer and ground cover demonstrates that fertilizer application doesn’t simply shift overall OSE abundance—it changes where along the ground cover gradient OSE reach peak density. This has important implications for management strategies, as optimal ground cover targets may differ between fertilized and unfertilized fields.
Simpler models (null, linear interaction, or single smooth) were poorly supported, justifying the inclusion of fertilizer-specific smooths in reporting and interpretation.

title: 2021 Locust × Ground Cover
text:
Unified model
\[
\begin{align*}
\text{OSE\_count}_i &= \beta_0 \\
    &\quad + \beta_1\, \text{fertilizer\_treatment}_i \\
    &\quad + \beta_2\, \text{mission\_number}_i \\
    &\quad + \beta_3\, (\text{fertilizer\_treatment}_i \times \text{mission\_number}_i) \\
    &\quad + \beta_4\, \text{region}_i \\
    &\quad + f_{\text{fertilizer\_treatment}_i}(\text{percent\_ground\_cover}_i) \\
    &\quad + b_{\text{farmer}_i} \\
    &\quad + \varepsilon_i
\end{align*}
\]

fertilizer_treatment * mission_number:

Captures difference before and after fertilizer application.
Models differential effect of fertilizer after application (mission_number 2/3 vs 1).

region:

Included as a fixed variable.

s(percent_ground_cover, by=fertilizer_treatment):

Factor-smooth allows ground cover x OSE_count relationship to vary by treatment.
Tests the “mediation” hypothesis.

(1|farmer):

Random intercept for farmers, controls for repeated measures and paired plot structure.

title: 2021 Locust × Temperature
text:
Overview
I checked how temperature varied across missions and regions. Fatick heated up through the sampling period, but Kaffrine, Thies, and Saint Louis were more stable. Saint Louis was generally colder than the other regions.
I then ran a GAM with a flexible smooth for temperature by region, including mission number and farmer as random effects. The trends were pretty similar to the original model, with the exception of some odd patterns at cooler temps.
To simplify, I also ran a model with temperature as the main variable and region/mission as random effects. In this case, both region and mission number came up significant for explaining OSE counts, but temperature and farmer had little effect.
Overall, it seems like temperature at the time of the survey isn’t a real driver for OSE counts once you control for region and mission—suggesting most of any pattern is noise or an artifact of timing/activity. I’m inclined to say temperature doesn’t need to be a focus in the main model, but happy to dig further if needed.









It looks like Fatick became hotter through the sampling period. Kaffrine, Thies, and Saint Louis seem more consistent between missions. Saint louis is definitely colder than the other three regions. So I would expect with the exception of Fatick, adding mission number to the model will not really add anything different.
Lets create the same model above with mission number included:
Seems like very similiar trends to the original model with the exception of more weird patterns in cooler temperatures.
